messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 57
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Architect
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 70

She is fifty-seven, an architect who has spent most of her adult life believing that careful planning can keep a life standing. She talks about buildings the way some people talk about family: load-bearing walls, hidden weaknesses, the importance of foundations no one sees. When she tells her story, it begins with her younger brother, the person she has always felt most responsible for, even though he is long past childhood and she is long past being able to protect anyone by wanting to.

He lives in another coastal city, not far in distance but far enough that visits have to be planned around deadlines and flights. He is a fisherman, practical and weathered, the opposite of her in many ways. Two years ago, during storm season, she is at her office late reviewing drawings for a civic project when her phone rings repeatedly. At first she ignores it, assuming she will call back when she finishes marking up a set of elevations. Then she sees it is her brother’s partner. She answers to the sound of shouting, wind, and a voice trying to speak steadily while saying that his boat has not returned when it should have.

She remembers very little in sequence after that. She says the evening fractures. There are calls to coast guard authorities, airline websites open on her computer, emails half-written to clients, and the awful unreality of still seeing neat parallel lines on drafting plans while imagining dark water. By the time she arrives the next day, her brother has been found alive but badly injured after hours in the sea, clinging to wreckage while another crew member drowns. She sees him in intensive care, swollen, bruised, breathing with effort. What stays with her is not the machinery but his eyes opening briefly and looking confused, as if he does not understand how he has ended up in this world instead of the one he left that morning.

He survives, but survival does not resolve the event. For months she flies back and forth, juggling project meetings and hospital corridors. She becomes the reliable one: speaking to surgeons, helping with insurance paperwork, arranging modifications to his home. People praise her competence, and she hates them for it. Inside, she is seized by images she does not want and cannot stop: his hands slipping on wet debris, his body disappearing under black water, the moment he might have realized the other man would not come back. No one describes these things to her in detail, yet her mind supplies them with cinematic force. At work, when consultants mention drainage, tides, storm loads, or marine corrosion, she goes cold. She excuses herself to the bathroom, where she grips the sink until the room steadies.

Sleep becomes thin and unreliable. She lies down exhausted but wakes around 3 a.m., heart pounding, convinced for a few seconds that she has missed another call. Sometimes she dreams she is drawing a staircase that leads directly into the ocean. Sometimes she hears her phone ring in the dream and cannot get to it. She starts charging it beside her pillow and checks it repeatedly through the night. During the day she startles at sudden weather alerts, sirens, even the hum of helicopter blades overhead. Heavy rain makes her chest tighten. She closes every blind in her apartment during storms, yet she also checks live marine conditions online as if vigilance might retroactively save him.

Before the accident, she had been known in her firm for mentoring younger staff and handling difficult clients with dry humor. Now she avoids site visits near the harbor and delegates meetings that involve waterfront development, though she gives practical excuses. She tells colleagues she is simply tired, overloaded, distracted by family matters. In truth, she no longer trusts herself in open spaces near water. On one site inspection she feels the wind rise and suddenly cannot breathe properly. She becomes certain, absurdly and completely, that someone is about to be swept away in front of her. She leaves early and later tells herself she is behaving foolishly, which only sharpens her shame.

Her marriage had already ended years before, but since the accident her life grows smaller in ways she barely notices at first. Friends invite her to dinners, weekend trips, gallery openings, and she declines because she does not want to explain why she keeps scanning exits, why she cannot tolerate cheerful conversations about sailing holidays or island ferries. Her brother is alive, and this complicates her grief. She feels she has no right to be as haunted as she is. When he says he is lucky, she agrees quickly, then goes home and cries with a force that surprises her. She feels guilty for imagining the worst when he is still here, guilty for resenting his partner’s calls, guilty for being impatient with his slowness and pain, guilty for being relieved whenever he does not go out on a boat.

In sessions, she speaks in the language she knows best. She says the event has made the whole structure of her life feel unsound. She used to believe that if she assessed risk carefully enough, she could design around catastrophe. Now she lives as if collapse is always one missed warning away. She keeps working, keeps producing elegant plans, keeps showing up in black linen and sensible shoes, composed to the outside eye. But underneath, her world remains organized around that night phone call, around water, around the knowledge that the people she loves can vanish between one ordinary hour and the next.
